'''Joan B. Berkowitz''' (March 13, 1931 – January 22, 2020) was an American chemist. Her areas of research included materials for the space program, reusable molds for spacecraft construction built from [[molybdenum disilicide]]s and [[tungsten disilicide]]s, and the disposal and treatment of [[hazardous wastes]].  She was the first woman to serve as president of [[The Electrochemical Society]].

== Biography ==
Born in [[Brooklyn, New York]] on March 13, 1931, Berkowitz attended [[List of public elementary schools in New York City|PS 42]], [[John Marshall Junior High School]], and [[Midwood High School]]. She created a [[science project]] analyzing weather maps from the ''[[New York Times]]'' to study the movement of weather patterns. She earned a scholarship to [[Swarthmore College]] and graduated [[Phi Beta Kappa]] with a BA in 1952. At Swarthmore she published her first paper, "The Preparation of ''[[Cis–trans isomerism|trans]]'' [[4-chlorocyclohexanol]]".<ref name="wcp">{{cite encyclopedia | title=Joan Berkowitz | encyclopedia=Women in Chemistry and Physics: A Biobibliographic Sourcebook | publisher=Greenwood Press | author=Klarreich, Susan |editor1=Grinstein, Louise S. |editor2=Rose, Rose K.|editor-link3=Miriam Rafailovich |editor3=Rafailovich, Miriam H. | year=1993 | pages=50–56}}</ref>

Berkowitz wished to follow her high school boyfriend and fellow Swarthmore graduate [[Arthur Mattuck]] to [[Princeton University]], but at the time Princeton did not accept women for graduate school in chemistry. Instead she attended the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]], graduating with a PhD in physical chemistry in 1955. Her [[dissertation]] was "Studies on [[Electrolytes]]", which focused on the application of the [[Poisson–Boltzmann equation]] to [[polymeric]] electrolytes. She used [[ILLIAC I]], an early computer, for the numerical solutions.<ref name="wcp"/>

From 1955 to 1957 she was a [[National Science Foundation]] postdoctoral fellow at [[Yale University]] studying polymeric electrolytes. In 1959, she married [[Arthur Mattuck]], who at that point had become a professor of [[mathematics]] at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. They divorced in 1977.<ref name="wcp"/>

In 1959 she joined the consulting firm of [[Arthur D. Little]], where she would spend over two decades. Her early work at the firm concerned high-temperature [[oxidation]] and materials for the space program, focusing on the [[transition metal]]s [[molybdenum]], [[tungsten]], and [[zirconium]]. She developed reusable molds from [[molybdenum disilicide]]s and [[tungsten disilicide]]s that were used in spacecraft construction.<ref name="wcp"/><ref name="NS">"Joan B. Berkowitz." ''Notable Scientists from 1900 to the Present''. Ed. Brigham Narins. Detroit: Gale Group, 2008. Gale Biography In Context. Web. July 7, 2011.</ref>

In the 1970s her work concerned environmental matters. She headed a team which created the two volume ''Physical, Chemical and Biological Treatment Techniques for Industrial Wastes'' (1976), a survey of manufactured goods and their potential for causing pollution. She examined [[limestone]] [[scrubber]]s that removed [[sulfur dioxide]], demonstrated how to reduce hard deposits which hindered their effectiveness, and improved their design. She also studied the disposal of hazardous wastes in [[landfill]]s and produced the first handbook on alternative disposal methods.<ref name="wcp"/><ref name="Illinois2002"/>  In 1979 she became the first female president of [[The Electrochemical Society]].<ref name="Profile">{{cite web | url=https://www.sciencehistory.org/historical-profile/joan-berkowitz | title= Joan Berkowitz | date= June 2016 | publisher=Science History Institute | accessdate=21 March 2018}}</ref>  By the 1980s she was a vice president and later head of the Environmental Business World Wide section at A.D. Little.<ref name="wcp"/>

In 1986 she left A.D. Little to become CEO of [[Risk Science International]]. In 1989 she co-founded with [[Allen Farkas]] the consulting firm [[Farkas Berkowitz & Company]].<ref name="wcp"/> 
In addition she has taught as an adjunct professor at the [[University of Maryland University College]].<ref name="Profile"/>


== Personal life ==
In 1959, Berkowitz married [[Arthur Mattuck]], a high school classmate who was by that time a mathematics professor at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. Mattuck and Berkowitz divorced in 1977. They had one daughter, Rosemary, who is also a chemist.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2010-07-04|title=Joan B. Berkowitz / Chemistry at Illinois|url=http://www.chemistry.illinois.edu/events/lectures/SM_Stoesser_Lectures_in_Chemistry/Joan_Berkowitz.html|access-date=2021-06-18|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100704105137/http://www.chemistry.illinois.edu/events/lectures/SM_Stoesser_Lectures_in_Chemistry/Joan_Berkowitz.html|archive-date=July 4, 2010}}</ref>

Berkowitz died on January 22, 2020, at the age of 88.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://magazine.swarthmore.edu/issue/summerfall-2020/their-light-lives-on/ | title=Their Light Lives on | date=October 11, 2020 }}</ref>

* 2005, Stanley J. Drazek award for excellence in teaching, [[University of Maryland University College]]  (UMUC) Graduate School of Management and Technology<ref name="Cox">{{cite journal |last1=Cox |first1=Gerry Vang |title=Women of Distinction: Joan Berkowitz, a pioneer for women, working in the field of environmental management |journal=Phoenix of Alpha Sigma Alpha |date=2005 |volume=91 |issue=2 (Spring) |page=17 |url=https://issuu.com/alphasigmaalpha/docs/asa_phoenix_vol_91_no_2_spring_2005 |accessdate=27 June 2019}}</ref>

* 1983, Achievement Award, [[Society of Women Engineers]]<ref name="Illinois2002">{{cite web |title=Sylvia M. Stoesser Lecturer 2002-03 - Joan B. Berkowitz |url=https://chemistry.illinois.edu/sylvia-m-stoesser-lecturer-2002-03-joan-b-berkowitz |website=University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign |accessdate=27 June 2019}}</ref>
